source: OECD (2025), Health at a Glance 2025: OECD Indicators, OECD Publishing, Paris
framing: Gap framing: every figure is what is NOT covered, NOT satisfied or unmet. Gap figures are 100 minus the published figure.
rule: HAL may phrase these facts freely but must not state any figure, ranking or claim that is not in this list. Verbatim report sentences may name other countries; only what they say about this country may be used.

facts.text: 49% of people in Poland were NOT satisfied with the availability of quality healthcare where they live in 2024, versus an OECD average of 36%.
22.4% of health spending in Poland was NOT covered by government or compulsory insurance schemes in 2023, versus an OECD average of 24.9%.
3.8% of people in Poland reported unmet medical care needs due to cost, distance or waiting times in 2024 (average of 28 OECD countries: 3.4%).
5% of hospital care costs in Poland were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 11% on average in the OECD.
25% of outpatient medical care costs in Poland were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 22% on average in the OECD.
56% of dental care costs in Poland were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 68% on average in the OECD.
64% of pharmaceutical costs in Poland were NOT covered by public or compulsory schemes in 2023, versus 42% on average in the OECD.
On the other hand, this share was less than two-fifths in Canada, Poland and Chile.

In Canada, over one-third of all pharmaceutical spending was financed via voluntary health insurance schemes in 2023, while in Chile and Poland, out-of-pocket payments financed 65% of pharmaceutical spending or more (see section on “Pharmaceutical expenditure” in Chapter 9).
The share was less than 2% in Poland, Luxembourg, Colombia and Türkiye, but stood above 5% in Switzerland, Korea and Chile (Figure 5.8).
In Mexico, the Slovak Republic and Poland, pharmaceuticals accounted for over 60% of OOP spending.
In terms of median number of days (Figure 5.11, right panel), this ranged from around 50 days or less in Spain, Poland, Hungary and Sweden, to 280 days in Slovenia.
In recent years, Poland has seen considerable reductions in waiting times.
In 2024, median waiting times ranged from 67 days in Sweden and Spain, to over half a year in Hungary (209 days), Chile (313 days), Poland (343 days), and almost two years in Slovenia (667 days).
Poland is again an exception, with large reductions in waiting times compared to 2019.
There were also two or less doctors per 1 000 population working in remote areas in Türkiye and Poland.

Across all staff types, positive perceptions on staffing and work pace are highest in Poland, Israel, Colombia, the United States and Latvia (50% or more with positive perceptions across different types).

In other countries such as Costa Rica, Poland and Germany, the majority of public funding refers to social insurance contributions – payable by employers and employees – which financed close to two-thirds of all healthcare spending in 2023.

Meanwhile, in Slovenia, Poland and Costa Rica, the role of government transfers in funding compulsory insurance schemes is marginal, with social insurance contributions representing at least 90% of all revenues of these schemes.
In 2023, Greece, Poland and Costa Rica reported the highest share of total health spending allocated to inpatient services, at around 40% – much above the OECD average of 28%.
Spending on general outpatient care provided by ambulatory providers was particularly high in Costa Rica, Poland and Mexico, reaching up to 14% of overall health spending.
This compares with the Netherlands, Costa Rica, Mexico, Poland and the United Kingdom where dental care spending represents only around 3% of total health spending.

With public health emergency measures phased out after the acute phase of the pandemic, the share of preventive spending dropped and reached pre-pandemic levels by 2023, ranging from 6-7% of total health spending in Canada and the United Kingdom to less than 3% in Poland, Belgium, Iceland, France, Switzerland, Portugal and Japan.
